title: 2 Samuel 17:23–29
context: Ahithophel, seeing his counsel rejected, goes home, sets his house in order, and takes his own life. David reaches Mahanaim, Absalom crosses the Jordan with Amasa as commander, and three men from east of the Jordan, Shobi, Machir, and Barzillai, bring generous provisions for David’s weary people.

verses.text: When Ahithophel saw that his counsel was not followed, he saddled his donkey, arose, and went home to his city, set his house in order, and hanged himself; and he died, and was buried in the tomb of his father.
verses.arminianNotes: Ahithophel, seeing his counsel rejected, goes home, sets his house in order, and takes his own life. Arminian readers read this soberly as the despair of a man whose trust rested in his own wisdom and standing, and they urge pastoral care for those in despair today.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the collapse of human wisdom set against God. Many interpreters compare Ahithophel with Judas (Matthew 27:5), though Scripture does not draw the link explicitly; the text records his death without comment, and readers should avoid speculating beyond it.

verses.text: Then David came to Mahanaim. Absalom passed over the Jordan, he and all the men of Israel with him.
verses.arminianNotes: David reaches Mahanaim, and Absalom crosses the Jordan with the army. Arminian readers note that Mahanaim was where Jacob met angels (Genesis 32:2), a place of earlier encouragement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers observe that Mahanaim had served as Ishbosheth’s capital (2:8). David now finds refuge in the place once used by a rival house, a reversal under God’s providence.

verses.text: Absalom set Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Now Amasa was the son of a man whose name was Ithra the Israelite, who went in to Abigail the daughter of Nahash, sister to Zeruiah, Joab’s mother.
verses.arminianNotes: Absalom appoints Amasa over the army instead of Joab. Arminian readers note the family ties, since Amasa was a relative of Joab and David, showing how the rebellion divided a single family.
verses.reformedNotes: The genealogy here differs from 1 Chronicles 2:16-17, which names Amasa’s father Jether the Ishmaelite and lists Abigail as David’s sister. Reformed readers acknowledge the difficulty and note that explanations vary.

verses.text: Israel and Absalom encamped in the land of Gilead.
verses.arminianNotes: Israel and Absalom camp in Gilead. Arminian readers note that the stage is set for a battle between father and son, a tragic outcome of choices made long before.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the rebellion reaching its decisive moment. The forces gather in Gilead, where God will settle the question of the kingdom. The two armies now face each other east of the Jordan.

verses.text: When David had come to Mahanaim, Shobi the son of Nahash of Rabbah of the children of Ammon, and Machir the son of Ammiel of Lodebar, and Barzillai the Gileadite of Rogelim,
verses.arminianNotes: Shobi of Rabbah, Machir of Lodebar, and Barzillai of Rogelim come to David. Arminian readers note the kindness of people who freely choose loyalty when it is costly.
verses.reformedNotes: Machir had cared for Mephibosheth (9:4), and Shobi was from Ammonite Rabbah, which David had conquered. Reformed readers see God providing help from unexpected sources, including former enemies.

verses.text: brought beds, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, meal, parched grain, beans, lentils, roasted grain,
verses.arminianNotes: They bring beds, basins, vessels, and many kinds of food. Arminian readers see generous hospitality that meets practical needs, a model of service to those in distress.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the abundance of the gifts. God’s provision for David in the wilderness recalls his care for Israel in earlier wilderness journeys. Bread in the wilderness is a gift.

verses.text: honey, butter, sheep, and cheese of the herd, for David and for the people who were with him to eat; for they said, “The people are hungry, weary, and thirsty in the wilderness.”
verses.arminianNotes: Honey, butter, sheep, and cheese complete the list, given because the people are hungry, weary, and thirsty. Arminian readers note the compassion behind the gift, attentive to real human need.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the providers acting as instruments of God’s faithfulness. Barzillai’s kindness is remembered later when David seeks to repay him (19:31-39). Kindness is not forgotten.
